sentence: Choose a polite greeting.
setupText: It is 9 a.m. You meet a new colleague at work.
taskText: Choose a polite greeting.
text: It is 9 a.m. You meet a new colleague at work. Choose a polite greeting.
explanation: 'Good morning' is a polite greeting when you meet someone in the morning.

Use 'Good night' when leaving at night or going to bed, not on arrival in the morning.
'Good morning' is a polite greeting when you meet someone in the morning.
'Goodbye' ends a meeting; you are just meeting Alex.
This is a goodbye about the next day, not a greeting now.

sentence: Ask politely to hear the number again.
setupText: A hotel worker says your room number. You do not hear it.
taskText: Ask politely to hear the number again.
text: A hotel worker says your room number. You do not hear it. Ask politely to hear the number again.
options: Can you say that again, please?
answer: Can you say that again, please?
explanation: 'Can you ... , please?' asks politely for someone to repeat words you did not hear.

rationales.What do you want?: This asks about the worker's wishes, not the number you missed.
rationales.Say it again!: This is a direct command. Add a polite request form when speaking to the worker.
This says you already know the number, so the worker has no reason to repeat it.
rationales.Can you say that again, please?: 'Can you ... , please?' asks politely for someone to repeat words you did not hear.

sentence: Choose words to thank the worker.
setupText: A shop worker carries a heavy bag to your car.
taskText: Choose words to thank the worker.
text: A shop worker carries a heavy bag to your car. Choose words to thank the worker.
explanation: 'Thank you for' names the help you appreciate.

'Thank you for' names the help you appreciate.
This asks for help; the worker has already helped you.
This apologizes for a problem instead of thanking the worker.
This welcomes someone to a place; it does not thank them for carrying the bag.

sentence: Choose a friendly reply to the thanks.
setupText: You hold a door open. A visitor says, 'Thank you.'
taskText: Choose a friendly reply to the thanks.
text: You hold a door open. A visitor says, 'Thank you.' Choose a friendly reply to the thanks.
explanation: 'You're welcome' is a friendly response when someone thanks you.

This usually accepts an offer; the visitor has thanked you.
This gets attention or asks someone to move; it does not acknowledge these thanks.
'You're welcome' is a friendly response when someone thanks you.
This is an apology. Nothing in this exchange calls for one.

sentence: Choose a short apology.
setupText: You step on another passenger's foot by accident.
taskText: Choose a short apology.
text: You step on another passenger's foot by accident. Choose a short apology.
explanation: 'I'm sorry' apologizes after you cause a small problem by accident.

rationales.Oh, I'm sorry!: 'I'm sorry' apologizes after you cause a small problem by accident.
This tells the other passenger to take care instead of apologizing for your own action.
This can accept another person's apology; here you are the person who needs to apologize.
This tells the other person an apology is unnecessary, but you caused the accident.

sentence: Choose a polite way to get the person's attention first.
setupText: You want to ask a stranger where the bank is.
taskText: Choose a polite way to get the person's attention first.
text: You want to ask a stranger where the bank is. Choose a polite way to get the person's attention first.
explanation: 'Excuse me' politely gets someone's attention before a question.

rationales.Listen to me!: This is a forceful command, not a polite opening to a stranger.
rationales.Where are you going?: This asks about the stranger's plans instead of simply getting attention.
'Excuse me' politely gets someone's attention before a question.
rationales.Come over here!: This tells the person to come to you and sounds demanding in this situation.

sentence: Choose a friendly, informal goodbye.
setupText: You finish lunch with a close friend. You will meet again soon.
taskText: Choose a friendly, informal goodbye.
text: You finish lunch with a close friend. You will meet again soon. Choose a friendly, informal goodbye.
explanation: 'See you soon' is a friendly goodbye when you expect to meet again.

This welcomes someone who has arrived; you need a goodbye as you leave.
rationales.See you soon!: 'See you soon' is a friendly goodbye when you expect to meet again.
This invites someone inside, not a goodbye after lunch.
rationales.How have you been?: This asks about your friend's recent life and opens a conversation rather than ending it.

sentence: Which greeting uses the name she asks you to use?
setupText: Your teacher's name is Ana Lee. She says, 'Please call me Dr. Lee.'
taskText: Which greeting uses the name she asks you to use?
text: Your teacher's name is Ana Lee. She says, 'Please call me Dr. Lee.' Which greeting uses the name she asks you to use?
focusKey: coverage-register-a1-3008:Following a stated form of address
explanation: This uses the exact title and family name the teacher requested.

She asked for 'Dr. Lee'; 'Mrs. Ana' changes both the title and the name.
Using her first name is friendly, but it does not follow her stated preference.
Her requested title goes with 'Lee', not her first name 'Ana'.
This uses the exact title and family name the teacher requested.

sentence: Choose an informal opening that uses his name.
setupText: You write a short email to your brother Ben.
taskText: Choose an informal opening that uses his name.
text: You write a short email to your brother Ben. Choose an informal opening that uses his name.
explanation: 'Hi' plus a first name is a simple informal email greeting.

rationales.To the manager,: This addresses a work role, not your brother by name.
rationales.Dear Sir,: This formal opening does not use Ben's name or fit the requested informal tone.
rationales.Hi Ben,: 'Hi' plus a first name is a simple informal email greeting.
This uses his name but closes a conversation rather than opening the email.

sentence: Choose a polite refusal.
setupText: A host asks, 'Would you like some tea?' You do not want any.
taskText: Choose a polite refusal.
text: A host asks, 'Would you like some tea?' You do not want any. Choose a polite refusal.
explanation: 'No, thank you' refuses an offer politely without needing a long explanation.

This accepts the offer, but you do not want tea.
'No, thank you' refuses an offer politely without needing a long explanation.
This asks for tea as a command, instead of refusing it.
rationales.Why do you want tea?: The host offered you tea; this question changes the topic to the host's wishes.

sentence: Choose a polite request for a coffee.
setupText: You are ordering in a cafe.
taskText: Choose a polite request for a coffee.
text: You are ordering in a cafe. Choose a polite request for a coffee.
explanation: A drink name followed by 'please' is a natural, polite order. An order need not be a full sentence.

This says you already have someone else's coffee; it does not place an order.
This describes what the other person wants instead of asking for your drink.
This command adds pressure with 'now'; it does not make a polite first order.
A drink name followed by 'please' is a natural, polite order. An order need not be a full sentence.

sentence: Choose a polite opening that names the hotel.
setupText: You answer the telephone at Green Hotel. The caller does not know you.
taskText: Choose a polite opening that names the hotel.
text: You answer the telephone at Green Hotel. The caller does not know you. Choose a polite opening that names the hotel.
explanation: This greets the caller and identifies the business immediately.

This greets the caller and identifies the business immediately.
rationales.Yes? What is it?: This does not name the hotel and can sound impatient.
rationales.Hello, is that Green Hotel?: This asks whether you have called the hotel; you are answering its telephone.
rationales.Hi! Who's this?: This asks the caller's identity but leaves your business unidentified.

sentence: Tell your friend politely that you must go now.
setupText: You are at a friend's home. It is late and you need to leave.
taskText: Tell your friend politely that you must go now.
text: You are at a friend's home. It is late and you need to leave. Tell your friend politely that you must go now.
options: Sorry, I have to go now.
answer: Sorry, I have to go now.
explanation: 'Sorry' softens the announcement, and 'I have to go' explains that you need to leave.

This tells your friend to leave; you are the person who needs to go.
This asks your friend to go away from their own home.
'Sorry' softens the announcement, and 'I have to go' explains that you need to leave.
This says you can remain, which is the opposite of your intended message.

sentence: Choose a welcoming invitation to come inside.
setupText: A guest arrives at your home. You want the guest to enter.
taskText: Choose a welcoming invitation to come inside.
text: A guest arrives at your home. You want the guest to enter. Choose a welcoming invitation to come inside.
explanation: 'Welcome' greets the guest warmly, and 'Come in' invites them inside.

This politely asks the guest to stay outside, which is not your intention.
'Welcome' greets the guest warmly, and 'Come in' invites them inside.
This sends the guest away instead of welcoming them.
rationales.Can I come in?: This asks for your own permission to enter; you are welcoming someone else.

sentence: Choose a polite offer to help the customer.
setupText: You work in a shop. A customer is looking at a coat.
taskText: Choose a polite offer to help the customer.
text: You work in a shop. A customer is looking at a coat. Choose a polite offer to help the customer.
options: You need to buy that coat.
explanation: 'Can I help you?' offers your help and lets the customer say what they need.

rationales.Can I help you?: 'Can I help you?' offers your help and lets the customer say what they need.
rationales.Can you help me?: This asks the customer to help you instead of offering your help.
This pressures the customer to buy rather than offering assistance.
This refuses someone else's help; you are the person offering it.

sentence: Choose a friendly question to learn the other person's name.
setupText: You meet someone at an evening class. You say, 'I'm Rosa.'
taskText: Choose a friendly question to learn the other person's name.
text: You meet someone at an evening class. You say, 'I'm Rosa.' Choose a friendly question to learn the other person's name.
explanation: After introducing yourself, 'What's your name?' is a straightforward friendly question.

rationales.Do you know my name?: This asks about your name, which you have just given.
This is a command to write, not a friendly spoken introduction.
rationales.Why are you here?: This asks the reason for attending, not the person's name.
rationales.What's your name?: After introducing yourself, 'What's your name?' is a straightforward friendly question.

sentence: Ask politely for permission to sit there.
setupText: There is an empty chair beside someone on a train. You want to use it.
taskText: Ask politely for permission to sit there.
text: There is an empty chair beside someone on a train. You want to use it. Ask politely for permission to sit there.
explanation: 'Can I ... , please?' asks permission to do something yourself.

This gives the other person permission; you need to ask for yourself.
rationales.Can I sit here, please?: 'Can I ... , please?' asks permission to do something yourself.
This invites the other person to sit with you; they are already seated.
This orders the person to leave their seat instead of asking about the empty chair.

sentence: Choose the sign that gives that instruction.
setupText: An office is cold. You write a polite sign asking people to close the door.
taskText: Choose the sign that gives that instruction.
text: An office is cold. You write a polite sign asking people to close the door. Choose the sign that gives that instruction.
explanation: 'Please' makes the direct written instruction polite and the action is clear.

This describes the door but does not ask readers to close it.
This is polite, but it requests the opposite action.
'Please' makes the direct written instruction polite and the action is clear.
rationales.Can I close the door?: This asks permission for the writer to act, rather than instructing people who read the sign.

sentence: Choose the greeting for your arrival.
setupText: It is 8 p.m. You arrive at a hotel and speak to the receptionist.
taskText: Choose the greeting for your arrival.
text: It is 8 p.m. You arrive at a hotel and speak to the receptionist. Choose the greeting for your arrival.
explanation: 'Good evening' greets someone when you meet them in the evening; 'Good night' usually ends the exchange.

At a hotel, this normally says goodbye at night or refers to going to bed; you are arriving.
This is a greeting, but 8 p.m. is in the evening.
This is normally a wish when parting, and the stated time is evening.
'Good evening' greets someone when you meet them in the evening; 'Good night' usually ends the exchange.

sentence: Choose a polite way to accept the offer.
setupText: Your colleague asks, 'Would you like a sandwich?' You want one.
taskText: Choose a polite way to accept the offer.
text: Your colleague asks, 'Would you like a sandwich?' You want one. Choose a polite way to accept the offer.
explanation: 'Yes, please' accepts the offered food, and 'Thank you' shows appreciation.

'Yes, please' accepts the offered food, and 'Thank you' shows appreciation.
This politely refuses the sandwich, but you want one.
rationales.Would you like one?: This offers a sandwich to the colleague instead of answering their offer.
rationales.Do you want mine?: This asks whether the colleague wants your sandwich; you have been offered one.
